title: Risk of Developing Subsequent Primary Colorectal Cancers Among Non‐Colorectal Cancer Survivors: Implications for Prevention and Screening

Improvements in early cancer detection and treatment approaches have shifted several common types of cancer from acute diseases with high mortality to chronic conditions requiring long‐term management [1]. There are now twice as many long‐term cancer survivors as there were 20 years ago with similar increases expected over the next 20 years based on current projections [2, 3]. One unique challenge for cancer survivors is that they carry a higher risk of developing a new or “subsequent primary cancer” compared to the cancer‐free population developing a first cancer [4]. However, little is known about whether specific survivorship groups are most clinically important and whether the absolute risks are high enough to warrant intervention. Approximately 15%–25% of cancer survivors will develop a subsequent primary cancer during their lifetime, thus contributing significantly to morbidity, mortality, and healthcare utilization [4, 5, 6].

Cancer survivors are at a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer (CRC) than the general population and CRC is one of the most common subsequent primary cancer sites to occur among cancer survivors [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. CRC screening has dual benefits because it can decrease mortality through early detection and can also reduce incidence through the removal of precancerous polyps. CRC incidence is declining faster than any other cancer in Canada and this decline is largely attributed to the implementation of organized CRC screening programs across Canada [10]. Despite cancer survivors being at an elevated risk for CRC, current guidelines typically recommend adult cancer survivors undergo CRC screening that is similar to the general population, with the exception of CRC survivors or those who received abdominal/pelvic/spinal/total body radiation therapy as a child/young adult [11, 12].

While there is evidence that cancer survivors are at an elevated risk of developing subsequent primary CRC (SPCRC), there are several evidence gaps that need to be addressed to determine if targeted/personalized screening guidelines for cancer survivors are justified. There have been few or no studies to: (i) evaluate if cancer survivors are also at an elevated risk of developing late stage CRC compared to the general population; (ii) evaluate if the risk of SPCRC varies during different survivorship ages (screening eligible: 50–74 and non‐screening eligible: < 50 and 75+) or during different periods after diagnosis; and (iii) identify risk factors specific to survivorship populations. Additionally, previous studies have focused on overall SPCRC risk, without analyses specifically on adenocarcinomas, which are the targets of screening programs and are used for determining risk stratification since they arise from precancerous polyps [13]. Therefore, the goal of this study was to examine the risk of and identify factors associated with developing colorectal adenocarcinomas among non‐CRC survivors in Alberta, Canada. This information is essential for determining the appropriateness of general population screening guidelines for non‐CRC survivors and for the development of targeted guidelines.

We conducted a population‐based retrospective cohort study of adult (≥ 18 years of age at diagnosis) survivors of a cancer diagnosis recorded in the Alberta Cancer Registry from January 1, 2000, to July 1, 2021 who survived at least 180 days following diagnosis. The 180‐day cut‐off was selected to align with the definition of metachronous (develops subsequently) primary cancer [14]. Patients were followed from 180 days after diagnosis until December 31, 2021 (administrative censoring), death from any cause, or the diagnosis of a colorectal adenocarcinoma. Survivors of CRC were excluded given enhanced monitoring for disease recurrence and screening for CRC. However, a secondary analysis among CRC survivors was conducted to provide a comparison to survivors of non‐CRC sites.

The Alberta Cancer Registry captures information on all cancer diagnoses in Alberta including data on morphology, stage, and diagnosis date, as well as cause of death and last known date of follow‐up captured via linkage to vital statistics. All cancer diagnoses are classified according to the International Classification of Diseases for Oncology, 3rd Edition and the International Agency for Research on Cancer rules for multiple primaries [14]. Cancers diagnosed in 2004 onward are staged according to the most recent Collaborative Stage Data Collection System from the American Joint Committee on Cancer. Since staging data are only captured beginning in 2004, our main analyses included all cancer survivors regardless of stage to increase sample size and follow‐up time for longer term outcomes. As these analyses account for time at risk of SPCRC, the results are largely reflective of early‐stage solid cancers and hematologic cancer survivors who have good prognosis.

Treatment information on cancer survivors was acquired via deterministic linkage to the ARIA‐MO (Medical Oncology) database. ARIA‐MO consists of electronic medical records for all 17 provincial cancer centers (2 tertiary, 4 regional, and 11 community centers) and contains data related to patient care including information on surgery, systemic therapies, and radiation therapy. Information on neighborhood‐level socioeconomic status (median income and urban/rural residence) was obtained using census information from Statistics Canada, linked based on the first three digits of patients' residential postal code. Patients' medical history and comorbidities around first primary cancer diagnosis (from 6 months prior to 6 months after) were assessed using information from provincial administrative data sources, including Physician Billing Claims, the Discharge Abstract Database, and the National Ambulatory Care Reporting System. Patients' body mass index (BMI) was calculated based on height and weight recorded during cancer‐related clinical visits within 6 months prior to 2 years after first primary cancer diagnosis; when multiple time points were available, the weight recorded closest to diagnosis was used.

The main analysis focused on adenocarcinomas of SPCRC; however, we conducted a sensitivity analysis including other histologies to be congruent with previous studies. The incidence rates (IRs) for SPCRC were estimated as the number of observed SPCRCs divided by the total person‐years of follow‐up and expressed as rates per 100,000 person‐years. Confidence intervals (CIs) for IRs were estimated based on binomial approximations using the exact method. Cumulative incidence function was used to estimate the risk of SPCRC, accounting for death as a competing event. Standardized incidence ratios (SIRs) were estimated as the ratio of observed SPCRC cases to that expected in the cancer‐free general population. The expected number of SPCRC cases was estimated by applying the IR of CRC as the first diagnosis during 2000–2021 among the cancer‐free general population to the follow‐up time observed among non‐CRC survivors. This was estimated as a weighted sum of the sex, age (5‐year age categories), and calendar year‐specific IRs for first primary CRC in the cancer‐free Alberta population. The difference in absolute risk was estimated using the incidence rate difference (IRD), which is the difference between observed IR and expected IR. The CIs for SIRs and IRDs were estimated using the normal approximation. IRDs and SIRs were estimated for cancer survivors overall (all cancer sites, other than CRC) and stratified by first primary cancer site. Cancer sites were grouped according to the definitions used in the Canadian Cancer Statistics reports and analyses conducted for the 23 most common non‐CRC sites. We also grouped cancer sites having a shared etiology with CRC by investigating obesity‐, smoking‐ and alcohol‐related cancers as defined by International Agency for Research on Cancer (Table S1) [15, 16, 17].

We carried out stratified analyses examining the risk of SPCRC by stage (I/II or III/IV), histology (mucinous or non‐mucinous adenocarcinoma), or topographical subsite (proximal colon, distal colon, and rectum). We also examined the risk of SPCRC by survivors' age during follow‐up (18–49, 50–74, or 75+ years) to understand if risk varied for cancer survivors within screening‐eligible ages (50–74 years). Finally, we examined the risk of SPCRC by the period of survivorship, stratified as 6‐months to 5 years, 5–10 years, 10–15 years, or 15+ years after first primary cancer diagnosis to determine whether cancer survivors were at higher risk of SPCRC during specific time periods. Cell counts < 5 were suppressed for privacy.

Exploratory analyses of potential risk factors for SPCRC incidence were conducted using Fine‐Gray models adjusting for the competing risk of death and reported as subdistribution hazard ratios (sHR) with 95% CIs. Sociodemographic and clinical information available within administrative data sources were explored to identify potential associations with SPCRC incidence, using complete case analysis to account for missing data. To account for the modification of cancer risk by attained age at follow‐up, age instead of time since study entry was used as the time scale of the Fine‐Gray models [18]. Cause‐specific hazard ratios were estimated for SPCRC incidence and all‐cause mortality using separate Cox regression models. Risk factor analyses were stratified by first primary cancer site, with results reported for survivors of seven common sites. Solid metastatic cancer survivors were excluded from this analysis since SPCRC among this group of patients is uncommon, their treatment patterns can be distinct, and they are typically not recommended for screening [19]. Inclusion of survivors in the overall study cohort and risk factor analysis is described in Figure S1.

The main model contained information on survivors' first primary cancer diagnosis, including age at diagnosis, stage (dichotomized as III vs. I/II or II/III vs. I based on site), presence of comorbidities, treatment modality (surgery, chemotherapy, and/or radiotherapy), neighborhood‐level income (above or below median), and place of residence (urban or rural). Specific comorbid conditions (cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and diabetes) were assessed in a separate model. A third model was built including BMI (≥ or < 25.0 kg/m2) and limited to patients with available BMI information. BMI data was available for 47,535 out of the 92,716 patients eligible for inclusion in risk factor analyses. All analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.1, R Core Team 2021). All estimates are reported with 95% CIs in square brackets.

Our study population consisted of 172,928 non‐CRC survivors diagnosed between 2000 and 2021 in Alberta, with roughly equal distribution by sex (Table 1). On average, females were younger than males at first primary cancer diagnosis. Median follow‐up time was 4.9 years (IQR: 1.7–10.2 years), with 68,382 deaths occurring before SPCRC including 38,985 cause‐specific deaths from first primary cancer. 1812 SPCRC cases were recorded, a majority of which were among males (n = 1102; 61%). The cumulative incidence of SPCRC among non‐CRC survivors at 5‐, 10‐, and 15‐years after first primary cancer diagnosis was 0.6%, 1.2%, and 1.6%, respectively (Figure 1).

Overall, there was an increased risk of SPCRC among non‐CRC survivors (IRD = 33.7 per 100,000 person‐years [26.3–41.3]; SIR = 1.26 [1.20–1.32]) compared to the cancer‐free population. The relative risk of SPCRC among non‐CRC survivors was significantly lower than that observed among survivors of a first primary CRC (SIR = 2.23 [2.04, 2.43]; n = 24,177). Among non‐CRC survivors, the risk of SPCRC differed considerably by site (Figure 2; Table S2). Statistically significant increased risk across SIRs and IRDs was observed among survivors of endometrial, head and neck, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), Hodgkin's Lymphoma, prostate, and breast cancers.

Sex‐stratified analyses showed that the IRD was similar between males (35.5 per 100,000 person‐years [23.7–47.8]) and females (32.0 per 100,000 person‐years [23.1–41.4]), while the SIR was lower among males (SIR: 1.21 [1.14–1.29]) compared to females (SIR: 1.35 [1.25–1.45]) due to higher observed and expected case counts. Sex‐based differences in CRC risk varied across sites; the SIR was higher among females for survivors of non‐Hodgkin lymphoma, stomach, or kidney cancer, and higher for males among head and neck cancer survivors (Figure 2).

A sensitivity analysis including carcinoid tumors in addition to adenocarcinomas found that SIRs and IRDs were slightly higher, compared to analysis of adenocarcinomas alone (Figure S2). In this analysis, lung cancer survivors were additionally identified as being at a significantly elevated risk of SPCRC, while kidney and NHL survivors had increased risk approaching statistical significance. Regarding inclusion of patients with metastatic disease, only 78 SPCRC cases occurred among metastatic cancer survivors and no site‐specific metastatic groups had elevated risk compared to the cancer‐free population. When combining first primary cancer sites by common etiology with CRC (obesity, alcohol, smoking), first primary cancers that shared a risk factor with CRC had a slightly higher risk (SIR: 1.31 [1.22–1.40]) than those without smoking‐ alcohol‐, or obesity‐related etiology (SIR: 1.23 [1.15–1.30]), although the risk remained significantly elevated compared to the cancer‐free population.

When examining the topological subsite of SPCRC (Figure 3; Table S3), cancer survivors carried the highest risk at the proximal colon (IRD: 13.1 per 100,000 person‐years [8.4–18.1]; SIR: 1.24 [1.16–1.33]), compared to distal colon and rectum subsites which had lower but still significant IRDs (5.0 [1.4–8.9] and 6.8 [2.6–11.1] per 100,000 person‐years) and SIRs (1.15 [1.04–1.26] and 1.15 [1.06–1.24]). When examining the histology of CRC (Figure S3), cancer survivors had similar SIR of non‐mucinous and mucinous adenocarcinoma (1.26 vs. 1.27), but higher IRD for non‐mucinous (27.9 vs. 5.9 per 100,000 person‐years). Breast and prostate cancer survivors had significantly elevated risks for both histological subtypes, while survivors of Hodgkin lymphoma, CLL, endometrial and head and neck cancer had elevated risks of non‐mucinous adenocarcinoma.

Among SPCRC cases with staging information (n = 1644), we observed that cancer survivors were at elevated risk of both early (I/II) and late stages (III/IV) compared to the cancer‐free population (Figure 4; Table S4). The IRDs of early and late stage CRC were 19.8 [14.7–25.1] and 10.4 [5.6–15.5] per 100,000 person‐years, respectively. The SIRs were 1.34 [1.26–1.43] for early and 1.18 [1.09–1.26] for late stage SPCRC. Survivors of CLL, endometrial, and prostate cancers were at elevated risks of late stage SPCRC compared to the cancer‐free population. Survivors of head and neck, breast, bladder, and cervical cancers were at increased risk of early, but not late stage CRC.

In age‐stratified analyses (Figure S4; Table S5), there were 37 SPCRC cases diagnosed among survivors aged 18–49, 954 among those aged 50–74, and 821 among those 75+ years old. IRDs increased with increasing age, being 8.9 [2.3–17.4], 26.6 [17.9–35.7], and 67.2 [46.6–88.9] per 100,000 person‐years compared to the cancer‐free population for survivors aged 18–49, 50–74, and 75+, respectively. In contrast, the SIR was highest among the 18–49 age group (1.67 [1.17, 2.25]). Because cancers diagnosed under age 50 were rare, the IRDs and SIRs were associated with wide CIs for most sites in this age group. For survivors in the screening‐eligible age range of 50–74 years, we observed significantly increased risk for SPCRC among several sites, including for survivors of prostate, endometrial, breast, and kidney cancer. Among those aged 75+, increased risk was observed for survivors of prostate, breast, and CLL.

Regarding the risk of SPCRC across the length of survivorship (Figure S5; Table S6), IRDs and SIRs were the lowest during 6‐months to 5‐years after first primary cancer diagnosis (IRD: 24.1 [14.2–34.6] per 100,000 person‐years; SIR: 1.20 [1.12–1.28]). The risks were steadily elevated over the remaining periods with IRDs of 44.9, 39.6, and 41.9, and SIRs of 1.34, 1.29, and 1.32 during periods 5–10 years, 10–15 years, and 15+ years after first primary cancer diagnosis, respectively. The risk of late stage SPCRC was elevated across all survivorship age groups, with statistically significant increased risk for those aged 50+ (Figure S6); similarly, the risk of late stage SPCRC was elevated across all survivorship periods (Figure S7). Finally, across subsites, the highest risk for late stage SPCRC was found in the proximal colon (Figure S8).

In exploratory analyses of risk factors for SPCRC among non‐metastatic cancer survivors (Table 2), we observed that overweight/obese BMI was associated with increased SPCRC risk among survivors of breast (sHR: 1.46 [1.01–2.13]) and head and neck (sHR: 4.48 [1.06–18.83]) cancers. Older age at diagnosis was associated with an increased SPCRC risk across all sites, although this association was not statistically significant for survivors of CLL. No significant associations with age were observed in cause‐specific models of SPCRC incidence (Table S7). Across most sites, females were at a lower risk of SPCRC compared to male survivors, with statistically significant reduced risk among female compared to male survivors of CLL (sHR: 0.36 [0.18–0.73]) and head and neck (sHR: 0.25 [0.07–0.93]) cancers. Additionally, in cause‐specific models of SPCRC incidence, female lung cancer survivors were found to have significantly reduced risk compared to males. Among lung cancer survivors, those diagnosed with stage I/II disease had a higher risk of SPCRC than those diagnosed with stage III disease; however this association was not observed in cause‐specific models due to a lower risk of all‐cause mortality for early‐stage survivors (Table S7). Lung cancer survivors who had cardiovascular disease were also at a lower risk of SPCRC due to an increased risk of all‐cause mortality. In addition, lung cancer survivors who received both surgical treatment and chemotherapy had increased SPCRC risk compared to surgical treatment alone, with significant associations observed in both competing risk and cause‐specific models; those who received only radiotherapy or no treatment had a lower SPCRC risk due to increases in all‐cause mortality. Among breast cancer survivors, higher SPCRC risk was observed among those who received surgical treatment in combination with chemotherapy (sHR: 1.84 [1.15, 2.95]) or radiotherapy (sHR: 1.49 [1.06, 2.08]), compared to those who received surgery alone; this association was consistent in the cause‐specific model. We observed a marginally elevated risk of rectal cancer among prostate cancer survivors who received radiation (sHR: 1.44, 95% CI: 0.99–2.08) (Table S8). No significant associations were observed between overall comorbidity status, urban/rural residency, or neighborhood‐level income level and SPCRC risk.

In this study, we observed that adult survivors of non‐CRCs were at a significantly elevated risk of developing colorectal adenocarcinomas, with a rate more than 25% higher than in the cancer‐free population. However, there was wide variation in risk across first primary cancer sites, with significantly elevated risks for 6 different sites. The risk of SPCRC was significantly elevated across age groups, periods after first primary cancer diagnosis, and for various subsites and stages of SPCRC. However, risk was particularly heightened among survivors older than 50, more than 5 years after first primary cancer diagnosis, and for the proximal colon subsite. Importantly, we observed that cancer survivors were at an elevated risk of developing both early and late stage SPCRC. The results of this study provide preliminary evidence that risk‐stratified CRC screening guidelines may be appropriate for certain groups of cancer survivors to address and mitigate their elevated risk.

Our findings are consistent with prior research which has identified an elevated risk of subsequent cancer among cancer survivors compared to the general population, with CRC being one of the most common subsequent primary cancer sites [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 20, 21, 22]. Regarding site‐specific findings, our results are consistent with prior investigations identifying a significantly elevated risk of CRC among survivors of Hodgkin lymphoma [5, 8], leukemia [8], endometrial [20, 21], breast [20, 22], prostate [5, 23], and head and neck cancers [5, 9]. However, our findings differ from several studies that have identified significantly elevated risk among survivors of ovarian cancers [5, 20, 24], which was not observed in our investigation. Due to SPCRC being a relatively rare outcome, further investigations making use of large national or international data may be needed to clarify the risk profile for survivors of less common cancers, such as ovarian cancer.

The need for improved screening among non‐CRC survivors is evidenced by our findings that there is an elevated risk of CRC for both early and late stage disease when comparing cancer survivors to the cancer‐free general population. Other factors used to identify high‐risk of CRC, such as having a first degree relative with CRC, have similarly elevated risk to that observed in our study (relative risk = 1.31 for first degree relative [25] vs. 1.26 for non‐CRC cancer survivors in our study). Although non‐CRC survivors had a lower relative risk compared to survivors of first primary CRC, it is more difficult to distinguish recurrence events from subsequent cancers at the same site, potentially leading SPCRC cases to be overestimated among survivors of a first primary CRC. Additionally personal history of CRC is already incorporated into screening guidelines for identifying high‐risk individuals who may benefit from enhanced screening; therefore, differences between CRC and non‐CRC survivors may be conflictingly influenced by increased monitoring, as well as preventive removal of precancerous adenomas among CRC survivors.

In prior investigations, patients with a SPCRC have been found to have a reduced prognosis compared to patients with a first primary CRC [26], demonstrating the increased importance of early detection and management of SPCRCs. Furthermore, the proximal colon subsite, which is associated with poor differentiation and worse survival outcomes [27], was found to be at a particularly elevated risk, providing yet another possible justification for the use of enhanced screening practices, potentially including increased utilization of colonoscopies [28]. Through implementing enhanced screening among targeted groups of cancer survivors, additional morbidity and mortality from SPCRCs could be mitigated [29]. In our study, survivors of bladder and cervical cancer were found to have higher risk of early compared to late stage SPCRC, which may potentially be explained by increased local imaging in the pelvic/lower abdominal region leading to incidental detection of CRCs that may have otherwise been detected at a later stage. Increased routine monitoring and screening implemented for survivors could lead to similar favorable shifts toward early detection and could further shift toward prevention, through removal of precancerous polyps. Future studies should examine the effectiveness of fecal immunochemical testing (FIT) among cancer survivors, as well as rates of adenomas versus serrated polyps (less sensitive to FIT) to determine if a shift toward colonoscopy for high‐risk cancer survivors is appropriate.

While there is a growing body of evidence on subsequent cancer risk among cancer survivors, there is less information specific to SPCRC, highlighting a need for more research to characterize high‐risk survivorship groups. Enhanced screening guidelines may not be warranted among all cancer survivors and should be limited to groups eligible for curative‐intent treatment who are at meaningfully elevated risk. The risk of SPCRC varied significantly by site, with the largest absolute differences among survivors of CLL, endometrial, head and neck, and prostate cancers. Additionally, older age was a predictor of SPCRC among a number of sites and survivors over 75 years old were found to be at the greatest risk. This suggests that enhanced screening during screening eligible ages (50–74 years old) may help mitigate this risk and continued screening after age 74 may be warranted for some older cancer survivors, depending on their prognosis and care preferences.

The elevated risk of subsequent cancers among cancer survivors is thought to be multifactorial, involving overlap between shared exposures or risk factors, genetic susceptibility, and cancer treatment‐related factors [30]. The elevated risk of SPCRC among survivors of endometrial, kidney, and breast cancers observed in our study may be partially explained by previously elucidated genetic risk factors, such as mismatch repair (MMR) gene mutations associated with both CRC and these primary cancer sites [31]. The mean age of SPCRC diagnosis among endometrial cancer survivors in our cohort was younger than other female survivors (69.0 vs. 71.6, p = 0.017), suggesting a potential genetic link. Furthermore, breast, endometrial, kidney, and CRC are obesity‐related cancers [32], indicating a potential shared etiology between first and subsequent cancer development in these groups; this is further evidenced by our finding that overweight/obese BMI was a predictor of SPCRC among breast cancer survivors. The lack of an association of BMI among endometrial cancer survivors may indicate a stronger genetic link and underscores the potential importance of reflex genetic testing and high‐risk CRC screening pathways among this patient population. Male sex was associated with a higher risk across first primary cancer sites, indicating that male cancer survivors may require more CRC screening than females.

Numerous investigations have demonstrated that patients who undergo radiotherapy have an increased risk of developing subsequent cancers compared to other treatment types [33, 34, 35]. Consistent with previous investigations, we observed a trend toward elevated risk of rectal cancer among prostate cancer survivors who received radiotherapy [36]. However, site‐specific associations between treatment modalities and SPCRC risk were largely inconclusive and impacted by differences in prognosis. While lung cancer was not strongly associated with the risk of SPCRC, we did observe that non‐metastatic survivors who received surgery plus chemotherapy were at an elevated risk of SPCRC compared to those who received surgery alone. Additionally, breast cancer survivors who received radiotherapy or chemotherapy in combination with surgery were found to be at elevated risk of SPCRC compared to those who received surgery alone. Although individual treatment‐related factors cannot fully explain the occurrence of SPCRC, there may be interactions among various contributing factors and differential effects across treatment dosages and durations, which were not investigated in our study. Future research is needed to more comprehensively investigate risk factors for SPCRC, particularly considering contemporary advances in radiation treatment which have improved specificity and may impact subsequent cancer risk.

In addition to considering development of tailored enhanced screening guidelines for cancer survivors, efforts to increase screening adherence may be beneficial for improving early detection and prevention of SPCRCs among survivors who are already screening‐eligible. Despite meeting criteria for undergoing routine CRC screening in Alberta, individuals aged 50–74 in our study had an elevated risk of SPCRC, including late stage cancers. In a review of adherence to CRC screening among cancer survivors, just over 50% of survivors were estimated to adhere to guidelines [37], well below population level screening targets [38, 39, 40]. The poor uptake of CRC screening among cancer survivors suggests that interventions to increase access to or improve awareness of the importance of screening in this population may be warranted. Furthermore, the elevated risk of SPCRC was found to persist for more than 5 years after first primary cancer diagnosis, suggesting efforts to improve adherence to screening guidelines should continue after patients have been discharged from the cancer care system. Strategies such as patient reminders or conversations with clinicians have been shown to be useful for addressing underuse of CRC screening [41] and could be important for delivering long‐term survivorship care after a cancer diagnosis.

To our knowledge, this is one of the first studies to comprehensively examine the risk of SPCRC by age, staging, subsite, and risk factors across survivors of various cancer sites. Our findings address an important evidence gap, being relevant for informing CRC screening guidelines tailored to non‐CRC cancer survivors. The population‐based data used in this investigation is of high quality, as the Alberta Cancer Registry has maintained the highest Gold Certificate status by the North American Association of Central Cancer Registries since 2005. Therefore, the completeness and accuracy of cancer incidence, mortality, staging and other clinical factors has high assurance. Furthermore, linkage of cancer registry data with other administrative databases allowed for the inclusion of important covariates, including survivors' medical history, cancer treatment and other characteristics which enabled more in‐depth analyses. Additionally, the incidence of SPCRC was compared to those without a history of cancer, which is a more relevant comparison than the general population which includes a large and growing population of cancer survivors (both CRC and non‐CRC). Despite these strengths, our study had limited power to conduct analyses for rare first primary cancer sites or sites which have poor prognoses. In addition, we did not have information on genetic conditions (e.g., Lynch Syndrome) in the baseline population or information on whether SPCRC cases were screen detected. Our results were based on observations from a population of cancer survivors in Alberta, Canada, which may have limited generalizability to other jurisdictions.

In this study, we have shown that there is an elevated risk of SPCRC amongst non‐CRC survivors compared to the cancer‐free general population. We have also shown that non‐CRC survivors are at an elevated risk for late stage CRC and subsites with worse prognosis. These findings are important for justifying and informing the development of CRC screening guidelines for cancer survivors, which in turn may facilitate a reduction in incidence and enable earlier detection of SPCRC cases. Further research is needed to validate which survivorship groups would meaningfully benefit from enhanced screening. Finally, efforts to improve adherence to existing guidelines for CRC screening may be useful to address the elevated risk of SPCRC among cancer survivors.
